title: Why latency falls off a cliff
sub: The same requests, arriving faster and faster, at one server.

frames.caption: One server, requests arriving at random. Each takes 1 unit of time on average, and time is measured in those units; the height is how many requests are in the system. At 50% utilization the server is idle half the time, and the line rarely holds more than a few requests.
70%: the same arrivals and the same job sizes, just arriving 1.4 times faster. Small bursts now leave a short line behind them.
80%: bursts take longer to drain, because the server has only 20% spare capacity to work them off.
90%: one unlucky run of arrivals builds a queue that lasts for a long stretch. Nothing about the jobs changed; only the load did.
95%: the line is now measured in dozens, and stays long for hundreds of job-lengths at a time. With only 5% spare capacity, a backlog drains at a crawl. This is the cliff.
Average latency, measured in multiples of the bare job time. At 50% utilization a request spends as long waiting as being served: 2× in total.
70%: about 3.3×. The curve is the M/M/1 formula W = 1/(μ − λ); the dots are long simulations of the queue above.
80%: 5×. A 5 ms query now takes 25 ms on average, and the slow tail much longer.
90%: 10×. Going from 80% to 90% load doubled the latency.
95%: 20×. The step from 90% to 95% doubled the latency again, and each step closer to 100% costs more than the last. Real traffic is burstier than this model, so real systems hit the wall sooner.
